claims.text: The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are equiatomic and sub-10 nm.
The as-synthesized particles are likely a metastable solid solution or amorphous.
Structural evolution during heating is driven by surface-energy minimization and rapid kinetic phase separation.
Surface-driven phase separation overrides the sluggish-diffusion behavior predicted for bulk high-entropy alloys.

The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down when particle radius is below a critical diffusion length and the surface-to-volume ratio is high enough for surface diffusion to dominate bulk diffusion.
For radii below 10 nm, the activation energy for surface diffusion is significantly lower than that for bulk diffusion.
Au has the lowest relevant surface energy and therefore segregates to the nanoparticle surface.
Pt has the highest relevant surface energy and therefore moves to the core or forms segregated domains.
Surface diffusion in sub-10 nm particles is much faster than bulk diffusion and invalidates sluggish diffusion based on lattice distortion and high activation barriers.
The smallest particles disappear by Ostwald ripening because their high curvature raises atomic chemical potential and rapid diffusion transfers material to larger particles.
Faceting or spheroidization is driven by surface-energy anisotropy as the alloy decomposes into Au-rich and Pt-rich regions.
Rapid phase separation into Au-rich shells and Pt-rich cores, or Au/Pt segregated domains, will occur within the first 100-200 K of heating.
Particles smaller than 5 nm will disappear through Ostwald ripening.
Surviving particles will become non-equimolar and exhibit core-shell or multidomain morphologies.
Effective diffusion rates will be orders of magnitude higher than in bulk alloys of the same composition.
High configurational entropy can stabilize equiatomic multielement solid solutions and is associated with sluggish diffusion and thermal stability.
For bulk alloys or particles larger than 50 nm, entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion may prevent rapid phase separation.
The segregation transition temperature depends on elemental surface energies and initial defect density.
The Ostwald-ripening rate is highly sensitive to heating rate and residual gas impurities.

contradictions.description: The breakdown criterion is stated as radius R < 10 nm, whereas the conditions and boundary use particle size < 10 nm. If particle size denotes diameter, these criteria differ by a factor of two.
